Report Highlights:   
FAS Mumbai forecasts marketing year (MY) 2026/27 India cotton area at 11.5 million hectares, a three 
percent increase from the previous year. Farmers anticipate higher fiber demand following recent trade 
agreements. Production is forecast at 25.2 million 480 lb. bales, a seven percent increase from the 
previous year and a three percent yield increase (to 477 kilograms per hectare), due to recovery from last 
year’s untimely heavy rains and expectations of a normal monsoon. Mill use is expected to increase with 
rising textile and apparel exports. The higher fiber demand will likely be met through imports, with mills 
continuing to access duty-free cotton under the advance license scheme. As a result, raw cotton and 
cotton yarn exports are expected to decline, while the focus shifts toward higher-margin, value-added 
products.

Area and Production 
FAS Mumbai forecasts marketing year (MY) 2026/27 India cotton area at 11.5 million hectares, a three 
percent increase from the previous year as farmers anticipate higher fiber demand following recent trade 
agreements. Production is forecast at 25.2 million 480-lb bales (32.3 million 170-kilogram [kg] bales / 
5.5 million metric tons [MMT]), a seven percent increase from the previous year. Yields are anticipated 
to increase three percent to 477 kilograms per hectare (refe r figure 1), due to recovery from last year’s 
untimely heavy rains and expectations of a normal monsoon.  Over the past month, seed cotton prices 
for the Shankar -6 variety (long-staple cotton) increased by four percent as the harvest season 
concluded and ma rket arrivals declined. Shankar -6, a Gujarat-based variety and the most widely 
traded cotton in India, saw prices firm due to tightening supplies in the market. Stagnant yields across 
major growing states and the government's reinstatement of import duties have further tightened supply 
and supported the price hike. Another factor influencing cotton prices is the rise in input costs such as 
fertilizers, pesticides, and agrochemicals driven by higher oil prices. Elevated oil prices tend to increase 
the cost of polyester fiber, which can make cotton relatively more attractive and support cotton prices. 
At the same time, higher oil prices also raise agricultural input costs such as fuel, fertilizers, and 
transportation as well as operational costs for textile production. India’s crude oil import price increased 
significantly over the past month, rising from around $69 per barrel in late February 2026 to about $80 
per barrel in early March 2026, reflecting an increase of roughly 16 percent. The rise mirrors global 
crude oil trends driven primarily by geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and concerns over potential 
supply disruptions.

Planted Area Estimates by Region  
North Zone 
For MY 2026/27, cotton area in Punjab is expected to increase by over 25 percent (to about 150,000 
hectares) from a low base as the state promotes cotton as a less water-intensive alternative to paddy and 
continues to provide subsidies and incentives for water-saving agriculture. In contrast, Haryana may see 
about a five percent decline in planted area as farmers shift to crops such as paddy or guar due to pest 
risks, irrigation concerns, and labor shortages for cotton picking, although yields are projected to 
improve by around two percent. In Rajasthan, planted area is forecast to decline slightly (around two 
percent) as farmers move to guar, maize, and pulses due to better price prospects, but improved pest 
management practices are expected to support higher cotton yields. 
 
As of mid-March 2026, the water outlook for the upcoming Kharif season in Punjab and Haryana shows 
relatively stable reservoir levels but continued pressure on groundwater resources. Reservoir storage in 
north India stood at about 52 percent of capacity as of  March 5, 2026, significantly higher than 29 
percent last year and 37 percent of the 10-year average, providing a reasonable buffer for the start of the 
planting season. However, falling groundwater levels remain a key long-term constraint, with deeper 
water tables reported at some monitoring stations. State governments are promoting water-saving 
practices and crop diversification, including incentives to shift from paddy to maize and increased 
funding for direct seeded rice (DSR), which can reduce irrigation needs by around 20 percent.

Meanwhile, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has warned of above-normal heatwave days 
from March to May, which could increase early-season water demand.

Central Zone 
Gujarat, the largest cotton-producing state, is expected to see slightly lower cotton area in the MY 
2026/27 Kharif season as farmers shift toward higher-return, export-oriented crops such as groundnut, 
cumin, and guar (refer figure 2). In contrast, Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh are forecast to maintain 
relatively stable cotton acreage, supported by established cotton-growing districts and continued farmer 
preference for cotton in rain-fed regions. Yields in these states may improve due to the growing 
adoption of precision drip irrigation, which helps mitigate risks associated with an erratic monsoon 
onset. 
 
South Zone 
Cotton area in south India is expected to increase by about 7–8 percent. In Telangana and Andhra 
Pradesh, acreage is likely to rise as farmers have greater confidence in assured procurement under the 
minimum support price (MSP) program by the Cotton Corporation of India (CCI). In Karnataka, cotton 
area is expected to expand. Declining maize prices driven by strong arrivals and excess supply following 
increased planting for ethanol are encouraging farmers to shift acreage to cotton. 
MY 2025/26 Production 
FAS Mumbai maintains its cotton crop estimate at 23.8 million 480 lb. bales (30.5 million 170 kg bales/ 
5.2 MMT), four percent higher than official government estimate of 22.8 million 480 lb. bales. Since 
October, the start of the Indian marketing year, cotton lint arrivals reported by CCI are six percent 
higher year-on-year, driven by increased MSP procurement as seed cotton prices remained about six 
percent below the MSP through March 12. Based on discussions with merchants and traders, the crop 
estimate is expected to range between 23.4 and 24.0 million bales. CCI data shows that market arrivals 
to date account for about 84 percent of the estimated production, even though seven months remain in 
the marketing year. However, FAS analysis suggests that historically 33 percent of the crop arrives 
between March and September based on the ten-year average, and 31 percent based on the five-year 
average, indicating that farmers may be holding a larger share of the crop that is not yet reflected in 
official government production estimates.  
 
Monsoon Outlook 
According to IMD, the seasonal outlook for March to May 2026 indicates above-normal maximum 
temperatures across most parts of the country, except for a few areas in northwest and central India. 
Rainfall during March 2026, averaged across the country, is expected to be normal at 83–117 percent of 
the long period/ten-year average (LPA). The LPA for March rainfall, based on data from 1971 to 2020, 
is about 29.9 mm. While cotton is generally tolerant of high temperatures and drought, prolonged heat 
combined with limited moisture can reduce yields, particularly in rain-fed cotton regions. Current 
projections assume a normal monsoon; however, early updates from global weather agencies suggest 
that El Niño could develop later in 2026. Although El Niño conditions are not currently active, their 
emergence during the year could weaken the Indian southwest monsoon, potentially resulting in below-
normal rainfall, higher temperatures, and an increased risk of drought and heat waves. 
 
Extra Long Staple Cotton 
Production 
Officials indicate that approximately 200,000 hectares of extra-long staple (ELS) cotton with a staple 
length of 32 mm and above are grown across central and southern India, primarily under DCH-32 and

MCU-5 hybrids, with production estimated at around 320,000 480-lb. bales (411,000 170 kg bales/ 
70,000 MT). Production increases remain challenging due to low yields, higher production costs, and 
increased susceptibility to sucking pests and bollworms.  
 
Consumption  
Post estimates an increase in MY 2026/27 ELS cotton consumption on improved international market 
demand. Mills rely on imported supplies, primarily from the United States., to meet consumption needs. 
The United States, Egypt, Australia and Israel are the major suppliers of this variety, and imports from 
the United States maintain an average 20 percent market share of total imports. More than 26 percent of 
U.S. exports to India by value is ELS cotton, and 90 percent of the imported U.S. fiber is re-exported in 
the form of contamination-free yarn and fabric. 
 
Stocks and Minimum Support Price 
The Government of India establishes an annual MSP for seed cotton, and CCI is the main agency 
appointed to manage price support operations if prices of Fair Average Quality grade seed cotton 
(kapas) fall below the MSP level. Procurement operations are carried out in Agricultural Produce 
Market Committee yards and CCI is sometimes assisted by other federal and state government 
marketing organizations (e.g. the Maharashtra State Co-op Cotton Growers Marketing Federation or 
MAHACOT) in cotton procurement. 
 
Procurement of cotton at MSP by the state-run CCI for the ongoing 2025–26 marketing season has 
crossed 13.4 million 480 lb. bales (10.4 million 170 kg bales/2.9 MMT), about four percent higher than 
last year’s 12.9 million 480 lb. bales (10.0 million 170 kg bales/2.8 MMT). Telangana accounts for the 
largest share of procurement, followed by Maharashtra and Gujarat to date. The procurement season is 
nearing completion, with March 13 as the last date for MSP purchases. Cotton procurement during 
2025–26 is likely to be the second highest since 2019–20, when the state agency procured over 13.5 
million 480 lb. bales (10.5 million 170 kg bales/2.94 MMT). Last year, CCI procured about 12.9 million 
480 lb. bales (10.0 million 170 kg bales/2.8 MMT). 
 
CCI currently holds unsold stocks of about 6.8 million 480 lb. bales (8.65 million 170 kg bales/1.5 
MMT). To boost sales, the agency has lowered its sale prices, as market prices have been trending below 
CCI’s offerings, limiting buyer interest. CCI expects sales to pick up after March as market activity 
increases. However, trade sources report that some of the remaining stocks have quality issues, 
particularly related to RD (reflectance), which measures the whiteness or brightness of cotton fibers and 
influences marketability. Consequently, CCI may need to continue offering discounts to offload these 
inventories, otherwise it faces the burden of large stockholding along with associated storage and 
financing costs. 
 
Marketing 
The government’s vision is to transform the cotton sector into a high-efficiency, premium global 
ecosystem by replacing water-intensive traditional methods with data-driven precision farming. Under 
the "Farm to Foreign" (5F) vision, the strategy focuses on doubling productivity through high-density 
planting (HDPS) and artificial intelligence (AI)-based pest monitoring while establishing Kasturi Cotton 
as a high-value, contamination-free international brand. To ensure farmer prosperity, the government is 
leveraging aggressive financial incentives including direct subsidies and an increased MSP to de-risk the 
crop and drive a sustainable shift away from paddy cultivation.

Realizing the government’s 2026 intent faces significant systemic hurdles. The main challenge is the 
pink bollworm's (PBW) evolution, which has rendered existing seed technology largely ineffective and 
led to yield losses of up to 30 percent. While farmers are seeking the latest pest-resistant cotton varieties, 
bureaucratic delays in regulatory approvals for new biotech seeds create a critical technology gap, 
forcing continued reliance on costly pesticides. This is compounded by an acute labor shortage and a 
lack of mechanization-ready, "short-duration" seed varieties. Existing Indian cotton plants grow too tall 
for standard mechanical harvesters, driving picking costs to an unsustainable 35 percent of total 
production expenses. Furthermore, the global branding of Kasturi Cotton Bharat is currently 
bottlenecked by a severe shortage of government-accredited testing labs, which delays the certification 
and geo-tagging required to fetch premium international prices. 
 
Consumption 
Post forecasts MY 2026/27 cotton consumption at 25.8 million 480-lb. bales (33 million 170 kg 
bales/5.6 MMT), about three percent higher than the previous year. The increase is supported by India 
signing key free trade agreements, which are expected to take effect by the next season. In addition, 
rising U.S. demand for Indian cotton apparels and textiles is projected to drive monthly double-digit 
growth in exports during 2026–27, according to industry sources. 
 
As of March 12, domestic cotton lint prices are aligned with the Cotlook A-Index. However, quality 
issues in domestic fiber and the duty-free import window through December 2025 led mills to rely on 
imported cotton. Since the reinstatement of the 11 percent raw cotton import duty in January 2026, 
textile production declined by four percent and apparel production fell ten percent year-on-year, 
according to the Index of Industrial Production (Quick Forecasts of IIP January 2026). The drop was 
driven by high international tariffs, rising raw material costs, and a temporary slowdown in consumer 
demand, with international brands placing smaller, fragmented orders instead of the bulk seasonal orders 
typical of previous years. 
 
Despite this, MY 2025/26 (Aug–Dec) cotton yarn exports by volume were four percent higher than last 
year and nine percent above the five-year average. A three percent depreciation of the Indian rupee, 
combined with a nine percent drop in yarn prices over the past three months, has made Indian yarn more 
competitively priced, enabling spinners to expand exports to neighboring markets. Major destinations 
between August and December 2025 included Bangladesh, China, Egypt, and Peru. 
Similarly, MY 2025/26 (Aug–Jan) cotton fabric exports by volume rose eight percent year-on-year and 
19 percent above the five-year average, with top destinations including Bangladesh, Nigeria, Sri Lanka, 
and Senegal. While both yarn and fabric exports increased in volume, the cumulative export value fell 
by four percent for yarn and eight percent for fabrics, primarily due to a global surplus of raw cotton 
depressing international yarn benchmarks and the reduction of domestic export incentives, forcing 
Indian mills to lower prices to remain competitive against duty-free rivals such as Bangladesh and 
Vietnam.

Exports 
 
Post forecasts MY 2026/27 cotton exports at 1.2 million 480 lb. bales (1.9 million 170 kg bales / 
327,000 metric tons), about 20 percent lower than last year. The decline is driven by a reduced 
exportable surplus due to strong domestic procurement, higher domestic consumption, and an increased 
focus on exporting value-added products. A continuing depreciation of the rupee could create 
opportunities for increased exports of cotton and cotton products. However, the government remains 
concerned about inflation amid ongoing geopolitical tensions, as rising oil prices are expected to push up 
freight and insurance costs. Although supplies may not be directly disrupted, shipping companies are 
likely to charge higher war-risk premiums, further raising import costs. FAS analysis of export data for 
February 2026 shows that raw cotton exports were down 51 percent by volume compared to the same 
period last year. In response, the government and trade are expected to focus on promoting exports of 
higher-value, higher-margin cotton products rather than raw cotton, aiming to capture greater earnings 
and improve competitiveness in international markets.

Imports 
Post forecasts MY 2026/27 cotton imports at 3 million 480 lb. bales (3.8 million 170 kg bales / 653,000 
metric tons), about 25 percent lower than last year. With the reinstatement of the 11 percent raw cotton 
import duty on long staple variety in January 2026, the government aims to protect domestic producers 
and stabilize local prices. Combined with the weakening rupee, higher freight and insurance costs, and 
slowed vessel movements, the policy has further constrained raw cotton imports, resulting in higher 
input costs for mills and limited access to cheaper foreign cotton. While the duty has been reinstated, 
textile exporters have urged the government to extend the duty-free period to address the need for 
sourcing high-quality fiber. Nevertheless, mills are expected to continue relying on imports to 
supplement insufficient domestic supplies of machine-picked, contamination-free fiber by utilizing the 
duty-free provisions under the advance license scheme. In MY 2025/26 (Aug–Dec), Australia, Brazil, 
and the United States were the top three cotton suppliers to India.  
 
Policy 
Cotton Duty Impact and Trade Opportunities 
In MY 2025/26, the 11 percent import duty on cotton, comprising five percent basic customs duty 
(BCD), five percent agriculture infrastructure and development cess (AIDC), and 1 percent social 
welfare surcharge (SWC), was initially exempted from August 19 to September 30, 2025, and later 
extended through December 31, 2025. The standard 11 percent duty was reinstated from January 1, 
2026. The reinstatement has increased input costs for Indian mills, reducing the competitiveness of 
cotton exports. With domestic supplies limited and sometimes lower in quality, mills are shifting focus 
toward higher-value, higher-margin products such as textiles and apparel rather than raw cotton, yarn, or 
fabrics. India’s textiles and apparel sector could benefit from several trade agreements that reduce tariffs

Government Initiatives to Boost Textile Exports 
The government is implementing various schemes to promote Indian textiles and enhance manufacturing 
and export competitiveness. The rebate of state and central taxes and levies (ROSCTL) scheme for 
apparel, garments, and made-ups (bed linen, towels, curtains, upholstery, carpets, and other home 
furnishings) supports exporters by applying the principle of zero-rated exports. Textile products not 
covered under ROSCTL are eligible under the remission of duties and taxes on exported products 
(RODTEP) scheme, along with other applicable export incentives. For more details, refer to PIB Press 
Release.
